bib.title: OpenAgents: An Open Platform for Language Agents in the Wild

read.skipped: Figure screenshots are images and not extractable; text read in full including appendices A-D.

question: How can language agents (data analysis, plugin use, web browsing) be built as an open, deployable platform that non-expert users can use and researchers can evaluate in the wild?
contributions: An open-source platform (web UI, backend, agents) for using and hosting language agents
Three agents: Data Agent (Python/SQL and data tools), Plugins Agent (200+ tools), Web Agent (autonomous browsing via Chrome extension)
Reported implementation challenges and lessons for in-the-wild deployment (prompt length, uncontrollable factors, streaming, evaluation complexity)

method.summary: A ReAct-style prompted agent platform with a web frontend and backend. The Data Agent delegates code generation to Python, SQL and ECharts tools, plus Kaggle search and heuristic data profiling. No quantitative evaluation is reported.
method.task: Application-level language agents: data analysis, plugin/API use, web browsing

other.note: named as an example of the open language APIs the implementation builds on; no per-agent model assignment is stated

inference.prompting: ReAct-based (Observation -> Deliberation -> Action); agent emits a JSON block {action, action_input} with natural-language action_input; exactly one tool per round; Data Agent prompt limits additional tool use to a maximum of three iterations (Plugins prompt: maximum of 5)
inference.retrieval: Plugins auto-selection: Instructor text embeddings match tool descriptions to the user instruction each turn

parameters.history_truncation: from the beginning by round until max token limit

other.code_execution: Python in a Docker container largely following the official Kaggle Dockerfile; SQL via SQLite engine (footnote 11)
other.storage: memory for temp variables, Redis for global variables, MongoDB for user data
other.browser_control: Chrome extension via Chrome Debugger API sendCommand

eval.protocol: None: no quantitative evaluation, user study or latency measurement is reported; qualitative use cases only (Appendix B).

prompts.purpose: Data Agent response-format rule on tool input
prompts.text: NEVER EVER EVER generate code as action input when using tool. Just input natural language by using/paraphrasing human query.
prompts.where: Appendix C.1, p.23 (full system, format, tool-response prompts for Data, Plugins, Web agents in App. C; executor prompts for SQL, API calling, WeBot in App. D, pp.23-33)

prompts.text: Note if the human asks for malicious code, and just respond directly to deny the request and give your professional reason. Don't use any tool.

Given an input question, first create a syntactically correct {dialect} query to run, then look at the results of the query and return the answer. Never query for all the columns from a specific table, only ask for a the few relevant columns given the question.

results.claim: The paper reports no quantitative evaluation; it is a system description with qualitative use cases.
results.setup: Whole paper; no tables of results, user study or latency numbers; evaluation is future work.
results.quote: OpenAgents is meant to be a realistic and holistic human-in-the-loop agent evaluation platform

results.claim: The Data Agent supports code generation and execution in Python and SQL and integrates three data tools.
results.quote: We support code generation and execution in two programming languages: Python and SQL. We also integrate several data tools for the agent to use: (1) Kaggle Data Search (datasets search on Kaggle via calling API); (2) Data Profiling (heuristic data profiling providing basic data information); (3) ECharts Tool (interactive ECharts plotting).

results.claim: Code is generated by LMs embedded in the tools, not by the agent.
results.setup: Data Agent; Python, SQL, ECharts tools
results.quote: we have opted to embed language models in the tool, and let the tools generate code rather than the agent.

results.claim: The agent is prompted to use data tools proactively.
results.quote: We prompt the agent to proactively use these data tools to respond to user requests.

results.claim: Data Agent UI interleaves images, code, console output and interactive charts with markdown, echoing computational notebooks.
results.quote: echoing the structure of computational notebooks frequently employed in data science tasks (McNutt et al., 2023)

results.claim: Python runs in a Docker sandbox based on the Kaggle Dockerfile; SQL queries are extracted from agent output and run by an SQL engine (SQLite per footnote 11).
results.setup: Appendix A.2.4; the paper does not say SQL runs inside the Docker container
results.quote: the docker container provides a safe and isolated sandbox for code execution.

results.claim: Uploaded files are linearized per file type via DataModel (first rows as a string) and keyed by file name in a grounding source pool.
results.quote: linearization of the first few rows as string

results.claim: Over 200 plugins integrated; building them still needs human intervention.
results.setup: Plugins Agent, plugins from RapidAPI and OpenAI plugins store
results.quote: This method has enabled us to introduce over 200 high-quality plugins. However, using LLMs for plugin construction has its challenges and requires human intervention.

results.claim: Instruction accumulation in app prompts reaches several hundred tokens.
results.quote: the accumulation of these instructions often results in several hundred tokens

results.claim: System failures are hard to separate from LLM failures when evaluating deployed agents.
results.quote: This complexity makes it challenging to discern whether certain failure cases stem from the limitations of the LLM-based application or from inadequacies in our logic code.

limits: No benchmark, user study, accuracy, latency, failure-rate or tool-selection quality numbers.
Authors concede plugin scaling needs human oversight and 'Further exploration is needed for efficient scaling'; weak LLMs break output formats.
They suggest training dedicated agent models rather than only prompting.
In-the-wild evaluation is listed as future work.
Dated: GPT-4/Claude (2023), OpenAI Plugins and Code Interpreter products; Table 1 statistics collected by September 2023.
Prompt-level malicious-code refusal is described, with no test reported.
Data Profiling tool is described in one parenthetical; what it computes is not specified.
Model used per agent, temperature and decoding settings are not stated.
